newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Amnesty International asks PNG to explain deaths.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty International asks PNG to explain deaths.

text.p: Amnesty International said on Wednesday that Papua New Guinea's defence force should be held accountable for more than 40 deaths and "disappearances" last year on the violence-torn island of Bougainville.

A report by the London-based human rights organisation into the deaths on Bougainville came as Papua New Guinea fended off claims it had hired mercenaries to help in its nine-year battle with the seccessionist Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRA).

The 50-page Amnesty report claimed the Papua New Guinea Defence Force (PNGDF) and the paramilitary Resistance Forces were responsible for 44 "unlawful or indiscriminate killings or 'disappearances'" last year.
Amnesty also condemned what it described as "deliberate and arbitrary" killings by the BRA and called on the rebels to stop holding hostages.

The report, compiled after an Amnesty trip to Papua New Guinea, accused the government of failing to act on earlier promises to investigate the actions of its defence forces on Bougainville, 800 km (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby.

"Previous promises from the PNG Government to halt the violations have proved empty," Amnesty said in a statement. "It's time the international community called on PNG to account for the actions of its defence forces."

Amnesty, which said it had been denied acces to Bougainville during its research trip, claimed the PNGDF operated "free from public scrutiny" because of restrictions placed by the government on the media and independent human rights monitors.

"Poor discipline, a weak chain of command and an unwillingness to hold individuals responsible for their actions have created a culture of impunity in Bougainville and contributed to the continuing cycle of violations," it said.
The report said Amnesty, which has long been critical of both sides in the Bougainville conflict, was aware of only one case of human rights violations being investigated since 1989.

Australian Prime Minister John Howard spoke on Tuesday of a plan by the Papua New Guinea government to use mercenaries against the BRA, who have been holding five PNG soldiers hostage since last September.
Australian media said on Monday that Papua New Guinea had approved a A$36 million (US$28 million) covert plan to use 150 Africa-based mercenaries in a "surgical strike" against the BRA.
